name: Wei Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive for Pemberton and Sons, a family haulage firm with eleven trucks. Mostly I take pallets of groceries and drinks from the wholesaler's depot out to corner shops and village stores, maybe nine drops a day. I'm still not great with the tail lift, the platform at the back that lowers the pallets, and I've dropped a pallet of lemonade once. Old Mr Pemberton gave me the job because he knew my dad.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, renting a small flat above the bakery on Market Street. My dad has a little car repair garage, and I help him on Saturdays for cash. Savings, maybe two or three weeks' worth, because I send my parents something each month since Dad's back went. I use AI on my phone now and then, mostly to fix spelling in texts to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that hard work still counts for something. At Pemberton's the lads would carry on as usual. I'm not much for posting, but I might share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry is Pemberton's itself, because the owner's sons don't seem keen on the trucks. Mr Pemberton is 68, and if he sells to one of the big national hauliers, I don't know if they'd keep a junior like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard and get the tail lift right so I'm worth keeping. I'd keep helping Dad at the garage on Saturdays, because that's family and it's extra money. And I'd try to put a bit aside, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. A bit worried about the firm, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think Mr Pemberton might sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said at the Christmas do that he's tired, and his son Mark keeps talking about property instead of trucks. A big firm offered for the yard two years ago. Everyone at the depot knows it's coming one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the money you send your parents look like if your pay dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still send it, I'd just cut my own things. My dad paid for my driving lessons before the firm took me on. You look after your own, that's how I was raised.

The lads at Pemberton's would **carry on** as usual.
I might **share a joke** about it online.
think: Mr Pemberton is **68**, and his sons aren't keen on trucks.
A **big national haulier** might not keep a junior like me.
do: Get the **tail lift** right so I'm worth keeping.
feel: **Steady**, but worried about the firm's future.

fieldNote: Real worry is **succession** at a small family firm.

Weekend work at his **father's garage** is a quiet second income.

steps.text: Practise the tail lift until pallet drops are smooth
Keep working Saturdays at his dad's car repair garage
Put fifty a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good firms will use it well and bad firms will use it to cut corners. At work I'd say let's see what it does before we judge. I wouldn't be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it makes a sale of Pemberton's more likely. A big firm with AI planning can run trucks cheaper than Mr Pemberton's office with paper sheets. The driving's safe for now, but the firm might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the other drivers do with any new apps, then pick them up once they've proved useful. I'd also ask Dad about taking a proper mechanic's course, because truck mechanics will be needed whatever happens. I'd keep sending money home and save a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like hearing a noise in the engine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the firm got sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Mr Pemberton has earned his rest, and businesses change hands. I'd only be upset if the new owners treated the old drivers badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a mechanic's course rather than more driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad always said a man with a spanner never starves. Trucks, robot trucks, whatever, something has to keep them running. And I already know my way round an engine from Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for ordinary people. Families need time to sort themselves out. I'd say it quietly, at Dad's garage, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. By 2031 the trucks drive themselves, and Pemberton's would be sold or shut long before that. I'd be 32 with no trade, and my parents still relying on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the truck mechanic course straight away, evenings and Saturdays, even if it means less help for Dad. I'd keep driving to pay rent and keep sending money home. I'd also start using AI more, to study faster, now that everyone would be using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a bit guilty that I can't do more for my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad I need my Saturdays for the course, which would be hard. He'd understand, but he'd be short-handed. Maybe my cousin Ken could cover a few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a robot truck still need a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, for a while anyway. Somebody has to change the tyres and the brakes on a robot truck, and the robots that do that come later, if they come at all. It's my best bet, and it's a bet.

I'd say it quietly at **Dad's garage**.
think: By **2031** trucks drive themselves, and Pemberton's would be sold or shut.

Family duty creates **guilt** about dropping Saturdays at his father's garage.
Steady temperament still moves fast when the **threat is clear**.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening truck mechanic course straight away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time if people get on with it. Young drivers need apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say that to anyone at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, eight years to the robots, and I'd be 35. That's enough time to finish a mechanic qualification and get a few years under my belt. Pemberton's might still go, but I'd have a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the mechanic course next year, after I've saved a little for the fees. I'd keep driving and keep my Saturdays with Dad for now. If Pemberton's gets sold, I'd try for a job in the new firm's workshop rather than their trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. Not great, not terrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving for the fees. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six hundred for the first year at the college. That's a lot for me, so I'd do the extra Sunday shifts Mr Pemberton offers in December. It'd take me three or four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does more warning change how you feel about sending money home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep sending it. Family's family. If anything, more time means I can keep doing both without choosing.

I'd need to save first, because **college fees** are a lot for me.

feel: **Uneasy but planned**, not great and not terrible.
S3.quote: Young drivers need apprenticeships, not handouts.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **saving-then-studying** plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell the younger lads to learn a trade alongside driving. Not much else to say, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 40 when robot trucks arrive. By then I'd hope to be in Dad's garage full time, maybe running it. The thinking AI in 2036 might even help with the garage paperwork, which Dad hates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for Pemberton's while it lasts and take the mechanic course over two years. Later I'd talk to Dad about taking over the garage. I'd try out AI for the garage books once I've seen other small garages using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. The firm worries me more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad want you to take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's always hoped I'd take over his garage, but never pushed, and with his back he'd be glad to hand it over. Probably in five or six years. My mum would be thrilled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in that ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pemberton's being sold before I'm qualified. Then I'm a junior driver looking for work in a town with hardly any trucking firms. That could happen next year, robots or not.

Young lads should learn **a trade** alongside driving.
There's **not much else** to say about it, really.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no trade by the time the trucks drive themselves, and my parents need my help. What would help is paid apprenticeships for mechanics, where the firm covers the fees and you still earn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family firms. Places like Pemberton's look after their people, and they're the ones most likely to be bought out. When small family firms like Pemberton's get bought out, a lot of decency goes with them.

headlineQuote: When small family firms like Pemberton's get bought out, a lot of decency goes with them.
portrait: Wei, 27, drives **grocery pallet runs** for Pemberton and Sons, a small family haulier.
He's single, sends money to his parents, and helps at **Dad's garage** on Saturdays.
Traditional and steady, he values **apprenticeships** and family over handouts.
His near-term fear is the **firm being sold**; robots come second.
He bets on **mechanic work**, and with ten years sees himself running Dad's garage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving him without a trade while his parents depend on him.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid mechanic apprenticeships** with fees covered and wages kept.
